tasks.title: Noon at the Olympiad
tasks.statement:
Yesterday, on October 16, 2015, the upper culmination of the Sun at the venue of the Olympiad was at 11:29:43 local time. Calculate as accurate as possible at what time the upper culmination of the Sun will be (or was) today.

Estimate the difference Ah in the height of the Sun at the culminations yesterday and today.

parts.question: Calculate the time of the upper culmination of the Sun today and estimate the difference in height Ah of the Sun at the culminations yesterday and today.
parts.reference: From the graph of the Equation of Time we see that now (and until approximately the first days of November) the apparent noon (the culmination of the Sun) every day comes a little earlier. We can find the rate of this effect by drawing a tangent to the curve of the Equation of Time at today’s date. We may get result that the rate is -30 minutes in ~5 months or about -12 seconds per day. So the the upper culmination of the Sun today will be at 11:29:43 - 00:00:12 = 11:29:31. The difference in height of the Sun at the culminations yesterday and today is equal to the value of the change of the declination of the Sun during the day, Ah = Δδ. Easy approximation of the declination of the Sun for the current season is δ = -ε*sin β, where ε ≈ 23°26', β is an analog of angle, 2π ∼ 360° ∼ 365.25^d, starting at the moment of the autumn equinox (this year it was at about noon of September 23). Assuming argument was days, and N was the number of days since September 23, δ = -ε*sin (2πN/365.25), and the daily variation is defined by the derivative of this formula: dδ / dN = -(2π/365.25) ε*cos (2πN/365.25). For today N = 24, dδ / dN = -0.37° = -22''. So the Sun today culminates 22'' lower than yesterday.

tasks.title: Eclipse on the Poles
tasks.statement: The White Bear and the Penguin from the previous International Astronomy Olympiads returned to their poles (North and South respectively), and decided to observe an annular solar eclipse. The Penguin was lucky to see an amazing picture: at the maximum phase of the eclipse the centres of both discs, solar and lunar, appeared just on the visible horizon. And what did the Bear observe at this time? Draw what the White Bear saw at that moment, and also contour by dotted line the true positions of the Sun and the Moon. Assume that the Earth is spherical. The drawing should include an artistic picture with an image of the Bear on North Pole; necessary sizes or angular sizes should be pointed out in the picture. Recollect for yourself the necessary information about the animals.

parts.question: What did the Bear observe at this time? Draw what the White Bear saw at that moment, and also contour by dotted line the true positions of the Sun and Europa.
parts.reference: It is necessary to take into account three important circumstances: physical horizon depression, refraction, and parallax of the Moon. Horizon depression for eyes at height 1 m is about 2'. Refraction at the South pole yields ~35', and at North pole about 25' (since the Sun is not at the horizon but higher). The parallactic displacement of the Moon is about 1.9° (12730 / 384000 = 0.0332 rad). Deduction: the White Bear sees the centre of the Sun above the horizon, at approximately 4'+35'+25' = 64' or about one degree. And the lunar disc is at approximately 1°54' below the solar one, i.e., totally under the horizon.

tasks.title: Close conjunction
tasks.statement: Some time after the events described in the previous problem (nobody knows even the order of magnitude how long after — minutes, or hours, or days, or years ...), Venus at the point of eastern elongation came to close conjunction with Mars, which was located near the aphelion of its orbit. At the same time a total lunar eclipse occurred on the Earth.

parts.question: Draw the corresponding scheme.
parts.reference: The corresponding scheme is drawn with angles: α = arccos(Av/(1+e)*Am) = arccos(0.723/1.093*1.524) = 64.3°, β = arccos(Av/Ag) = 43.7°, γ = 72°.

parts.question: Explain, which animal (sitting at the same poles) may see this lunar eclipse. (At the very end of your explanation write as answer B+ or B- for the Bear and P+ or P- for the Penguin.) An artistic picture of the observations of the animals is welcome.
parts.reference: The situation corresponds to the middle of June. At this time the Sun is shining for the Bear at the North pole, and the Moon (that is in the opposite point of the celestial sphere at the moment of eclipse) may be observed by Penguin at the South pole. Answer: B— P+.

parts.question: Calculate in which constellation the eclipsed Moon was observed.
parts.reference: Mars in aphelion/perihelion relation: direction corresponds to Sun>Earth 72° earlier, i.e., 71 days earlier, for June 15. By the sky map we may find that this direction is to a point in Ophiuchus constellation just near to the border with Sagittarius.

parts.question: Estimate minimal possible time passed from the situation of the previous problem to the situation of the current one.
parts.reference: The orbital nodes of the Moon move with period 18.6 years. The minimum possible time may be in the case the line of nodes moved from end September - end March line to middle June - middle December line, that is about 28% of the period or 18.6 * 0.28 = 5.2 years. Precise synodic periods calculation leads to about 5 years and 3 months (e.g., June 5, 2020).

tasks.title: Alpha Centauri
tasks.statement: Calculate, which star emits more energy: the Sun or Alpha Centauri A+B.

parts.question: Calculate, which star emits more energy: the Sun or Alpha Centauri A+B.
parts.reference: Let us calculate the apparent magnitude of Alpha Centauri A, if it was located at the place of the Sun, m_acenA' = m_acenA + 5*lg((pc/au)/p_acen) = -0.01'' + 5 - lg(206265'' / 0.747'') = -27.22''. This value is smaller than that of the Sun (-26.8''). Then Alpha Centauri A radiates more energy. Adding radiation of Alpha Centauri B, Alpha Centauri A+B emits more energy than the Sun.

tasks.title: Motion of a satellite
tasks.statement: An artificial Satellite, moving in equatorial, slightly elliptical orbit passed the perigee point at the height of Hp = 428.0 km from the sea level; and its speed at the point was 0.6% higher than the circumferential velocity of the given point. Find the time after which the satellite will reach the height Ha = 498.0 km?

parts.question: Find the time after which the satellite will reach the height Ha = 498.0 km.
parts.reference: Working in the frame of reference rotating around the Earth along with the satellite, the satellite is affected by centrifugal and gravitational forces. Acceleration a = (Fc - Fg)/m = (V_1^2 - V_0^2)/R = (1.006^2 - 1^2)*g_0 = 0.012*g_0 * [R_0 / (R_0+H)]^2 ≈ 0.103 m/s^2. From the formula ΔH = a*t^2/2, the time to reach the height H_a is t = (2ΔH/a)^(1/2), which is about 1160 seconds or 19.4 minutes.
